messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 37-year-old Ghanaian-American psychologist who presents to therapy following what he describes, with visible difficulty, as "something I've spent two years trying to outthink." He is single, soft-spoken, and carries himself with the careful composure of someone accustomed to being the most regulated person in the room. That composure, he acknowledges, has become harder to maintain.

Two years ago, Kofi attended a professional conference in a mid-sized city several states from his home. After an evening social event, a colleague he had known for several years offered to continue a conversation in his hotel room. What followed was a rape. The door was locked from the inside — Kofi remembers the sound of the deadbolt, the way the room seemed to contract around him, the realisation that his professional familiarity with this man had given him no protection at all. He did not disclose to conference staff. He drove home two days later and returned to his caseload the following Monday.

In the months after, the memory did not organise itself into a coherent past event. Instead it arrived in fragments — sensory, sudden, and without warning. The click of a lock. A colleague's offhand remark during a case consultation about a client's sexual assault. These moments would rupture the ordinary texture of his day without transition or preparation. He found himself unable to place the memory as something that had already ended.

Kofi's work as a psychologist means he sits with clients for fifty-minute hours in small, closed offices. He began requesting that consultation rooms be left slightly ajar, offering clinical rationales his supervisors accepted without question. When a building policy required doors to be shut during sessions, he found himself conducting the hour with his chair angled toward the exit, his back pressed to the wall behind him, scanning the room in a way he recognised clinically but could not interrupt. He has not been able to fall asleep before two or three in the morning for the better part of eighteen months, lying in the particular alertness of someone who does not believe the night is finished with them yet. Even on weekends, in his own apartment, with no appointment to keep, the loosening that other people called rest did not come.

He had also begun to reorganise his professional and social life around the fact of other men. He no longer accepted one-on-one supervision from male colleagues, citing scheduling conflicts. He declined invitations to small gatherings if he could not be certain of the composition of the room. When these arrangements failed — when he found himself alone with a male client, or walking to his car with a male coworker — something in him registered the situation as structurally identical to the hotel room, regardless of what he knew.

What has accumulated alongside these adjustments is a set of beliefs about himself that Kofi finds, professionally, he cannot simply reframe away. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that what happened to him was somehow visible — that colleagues who looked at him a beat too long were seeing it, that clients sensed something compromised in him, that the professional authority he had spent a decade building was now a performance others could see through. He was certain that bad things would continue to find him, that his history had marked him as someone without the capacity to prevent his own harm. When he tried to imagine his life five or ten years forward — a question he routinely asked his own clients — he found nothing there. Not grief, not fear of a specific outcome. Simply an absence.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a session three weeks ago in which a client disclosed a recent sexual assault. He sat with her for the remainder of the hour, reflected her experience back with skill, made the appropriate safety referrals. Afterward, alone in his office with the door open, he understood that he could not continue to offer to others what he was not able to reach for himself. He arrives now hoping, tentatively, that the absence where his future should be might not be permanent. What he fears most is that a therapist will look at him and see exactly what he sees when he looks in the mirror.
